1.note: The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [everything about Yahweh]

2.note: The psalmist is speaking of the temple where Yahweh is worshiped as if it were a house in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the temple of Yahweh]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [who are standing in the courts of the house of]

By using this possessive form, **our God**, the psalmist is not saying that the Israelites possess or control Yahweh. Rather he is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the Israelites worship. See the introduction to Psalms for further discussion. Alternate translation: [the God whom we worship]

3.note: The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]
Here, **his name** represents who Yahweh is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [to Yahweh]

4.note: **Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the name **Jacob** to refer to the people of Israel who were all descendants of the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he chose Israel for his special possession]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **possession**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as his own special people]

5.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I know** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize how confident he is in this knowledge. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I definitely know]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and our Lord is greater than all gods]
The term “god,” when applied to a being other than Yahweh, can refer to an idol, but, as here, it can also refer to any lesser spirit being. Alternate translation: [than any other spiritual being]

6.note: The psalmist is referring to everywhere in all of creation by naming two pairs of extremes, **the heavens** and **the earth**, as well as **the seas** and **all deeps**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everywhere in all of creation]

7.note: Here the word translated **bringing up** does not have an explicit subject. The context of the previous verse makes clear that the subject is Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is bringing up clouds from the end of the earth]

The psalmist is using the phrase **from the end of the earth** as a common expression to mean “from distant places.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from everywhere on earth]

The psalmist is speaking of wind as if it were kept in **storehouses**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from where he has prepared it]

8.note: The word **who** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh struck the firstborn of Egypt]
Here, **struck** represents to kill or slaughter. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as modeled in the UST.

The psalmist is referring to all living beings by naming two extremes, **man** and **beast**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of every kind of creature of Egypt]

9.note: The terms **signs** and **wonders** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [extraordinary demonstrations of his power]

The psalmist is speaking to **Egypt**, which cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about what God did there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Egypt. Alternate translation: [right in front of the Egyptians]

10.note: The word **who** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh struck many nations]
Here, **struck** represents killing or defeating in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who conquered]

11.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He defeated Sihon, king of the Amorite]

12.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, while the word **their** refers to the defeated kings mentioned in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh gave the land of those kings]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to them as a gift to inherit]

13.q: יְ֭הוָה שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֣ לְ⁠עוֹלָ֑ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה זִכְרְ⁠ךָ֥ לְ⁠דֹר־וָ⁠דֹֽר
13.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, you will be known and remembered through every generation] or [Yahweh, your name is to forever, indeed, your remembrance is to generation and generation]

Here, **name** represents Yahweh’s reputation and character. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [your reputation]

The psalmist is using **to forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “eternally” or “without end.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [lasts throughout eternity]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remembrance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people will remember you from generation to generation]

The psalmist is using the phrase **to generation and generation** as a common expression to mean “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is through all generations] or [is forever]

14.note: The word **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

15.note: Here, **the hands of man** represents the craftsmanship and ability of people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [the work of men] or [made by men]

16.q: פֶּֽה־לָ֭⁠הֶם וְ⁠לֹ֣א יְדַבֵּ֑רוּ עֵינַ֥יִם לָ֝⁠הֶ֗ם וְ⁠לֹ֣א יִרְאֽוּ
16.note: See how you translated the same phrases in Psalm 115:5.

17.note: See how you translated the similar phrase, “ears are to them, but they do not hear” in Psalm 115:6.

18.q: כְּ֭מוֹ⁠הֶם יִהְי֣וּ עֹשֵׂי⁠הֶ֑ם כֹּ֭ל אֲשֶׁר־בֹּטֵ֣חַ בָּ⁠הֶֽם
18.note: See how you translated the same phrases in Psalm 115:8.

19.note: Here, **House** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **House of Israel** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [People of Israel]
Here the psalmist is using the word **house** to mean all the people descended from Aaron. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.

20.note: Here the psalmist is using the word **House** to mean all the people descended from Levi. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All you Levites]

21.note: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the worshippers of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [May we bless Yahweh from Zion]
Here, **the one** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [who dwells in Jerusalem]
